How this book matches your board exam. Research check: this book follows NCERT Class 12 Mathematics, Chapter 1 (Relations and Functions) and Chapter 2 (Inverse Trigonometric Functions), for the CBSE 2026–27 session. Unit I, Relations and Functions, carries 8 marks. The syllabus covers types of relations (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, equivalence), one-one and onto functions, and the definition, domain, range, principal value branches and graphs of inverse trigonometric functions. (Composite functions, inverse of a function, binary operations and the properties of inverse trigonometric functions are not in the current syllabus.)

The theory paper is 80 marks in 3 hours, with 20 internal marks. Recent sample papers have 38 questions in five sections: A — 20 one-mark items (18 MCQs + 2 assertion–reason); B — 5 two-mark; C — 6 three-mark; D — 4 five-mark; E — 3 four-mark case-based.

Each unit ends with a 10-mark practice set. Every answer was checked by computer. The marking points are our own, not the official CBSE marking scheme.

Unit 1 of 10: Relations and Their Types

Key ideas

  • A relation R from a set A to a set B is a subset of A × B. A relation on A is a subset of A × A.
  • Empty relation: no element of A is related to any element, R = ∅ ⊂ A × A. Universal relation: every element is related to every element, R = A × A. Both are called trivial relations.
  • A relation R on A is:
  • reflexive if (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A;
  • symmetric if (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R;
  • transitive if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R.
  • To disprove a property, give one counter-example. To prove it, argue for general elements.

Worked examples

Example 1: On A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2)}. Answer: reflexive (all (a, a) present); not symmetric ((1, 2) ∈ R but (2, 1) ∉ R); transitive (the only chains are trivial, e.g. (1, 1), (1, 2) ⇒ (1, 2) ✓).

Example 2: R = {(a, b) : a ≤ b} on the real numbers. Answer: reflexive (a ≤ a); not symmetric (1 ≤ 2 but 2 ≰ 1); transitive (a ≤ b, b ≤ c ⇒ a ≤ c).

Example 3: R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)} on A = {1, 2, 3}. Answer: not reflexive; symmetric; not transitive, since (1, 2), (2, 1) ∈ R but (1, 1) ∉ R.

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark, MCQ) The relation R = {(1, 1), (2, 2)} on A = {1, 2, 3} is: (a) reflexive (b) symmetric and transitive but not reflexive (c) an equivalence relation (d) universal. Answer: (b).
  2. (1 mark) Is the empty relation on A = {1, 2} reflexive? Answer: no, since (1, 1) ∉ R.
  3. (2 marks) Check whether R = {(a, b) : b = a + 1} on A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} is reflexive or symmetric. Answer: not reflexive, as (1, 1) ∉ R (1); not symmetric, as (1, 2) ∈ R but (2, 1) ∉ R (1).
  4. (3 marks) Show that R = {(a, b) : a ≤ b²} on the real numbers is neither reflexive nor symmetric nor transitive. Answer: not reflexive: (½, ½) ∉ R since ½ > ¼ (1); not symmetric: (1, 4) ∈ R but (4, 1) ∉ R since 4 > 1 (1); not transitive: (3, 2), (2, 1.5) ∈ R (3 ≤ 4 and 2 ≤ 2.25) but (3, 1.5) ∉ R since 3 > 2.25 (1).
  5. (3 marks) Let A = {1, 2, 3}. Write the smallest relation on A that is reflexive and contains (1, 2) and (2, 3), and check whether it is transitive. Answer: R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 3)} (1); (1, 2), (2, 3) ∈ R but (1, 3) ∉ R (1); so it is not transitive (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Checking reflexivity on a few elements only. 2. Calling a relation transitive without checking all chains. 3. Using a "proof" by example for a general property. 4. Forgetting that (1, 2), (2, 1) forces (1, 1) for transitivity. 5. Confusing the empty relation with the universal one.

Quick recall

  1. Reflexive means? 2. Symmetric means? 3. Transitive means? 4. Universal relation on A? 5. How to disprove a property?

Answers: 1) (a, a) ∈ R for all a. 2) (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R. 3) (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R. 4) A × A. 5) One counter-example.
